question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, on Evans' view essentially yes, and with the universal quantifier in hand yes in the closed form too.

For Evans a singular thought Fa is not a brute particularistic attachment of F to a. To think Fa you have to think of a under a mode of presentation which is the concept F. To possess F as a concept is to be able to deploy it generally. The Generality Constraint is that a way of thinking that is available for a must be available for any object that could be that way of thinking. 

Hence if you can entertain Fa you must be able to entertain the thought `x is F` with x free for arbitrary substitution. That is the minimal generalizability required by having F as a general concept at all. Once you have that free-variable schema you can close it with the quantifier you already understand. Understanding `∀x` is understanding the closure of the schema `x is F`. 

So understanding Fa already commits you to having F as a general concept and therefore to being able to think the open sentence Fx for arbitrary x. If, as stipulated, you understand universal quantification, you can then understand the closed proposition ∀x Fx as the universal closure of that schema. The constraint does not by itself entail that you believe ∀x Fx is true, only that you must be able to make sense of, i.e. think, the generalization of the concept you deploy in Fa. Having a non-generalizable mode of presentation of F of a would be exactly the kind of singular, non-substitutable thought Evans rules out.

5.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the possession of concepts, not on what you know about the world.

If you can entertain the singular thought Fa then, on Evans' picture, you do not have a piece of singular information about a that is insulated from the rest of your conceptual economy. In order to think of a as F you must possess F as a general concept which can be deployed for arbitrary objects. The thought Fa therefore commits you to having the schematic thought Fx and the capacity to apply F to any object you can identify.

Once that general concept F is possessed, and you are independently in command of universal quantification, you are in a position to grasp the meaning of the closed sentence

∀x Fx

i.e. to see what would have to be the case for it to be true and to see what would have to be the case for it to be false. That is all that is required for understanding the sentence. It does not commit you to the truth of ∀x Fx, nor does understanding Fa give you any epistemic warrant for asserting it. Understanding Fa only gives you the general concept F and, with quantificational competence, the capacity to entertain the universal generalisation as a proposition you can evaluate. The Generality Constraint rules out a genuinely singular, non-generalizable grasp of F supplied by Fa.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans’ Gener­ality Constraint the content of a singular thought about a is not tied to a particular mode of presentation of a; to think Fa at all is to be able to think of a under the concept F in a way that can be operated on in the same inferential system as any other thinkable object of thought. That is, understanding Fa commits you to having an understanding of the general predicate F as an open formula, Fx, with a as a permissible value for x. You are not permitted to grasp F-of-a in isolation from the general concept F that you can apply to any object you can think about.

If you already understand universal quantification, then the closure of that open formula is ipso facto intelligible to you. Fx is the general mode in which F is available to thought, and ∀x Fx is just the fully general deployment of that same mode. The Gener­ality Constraint is precisely the demand that the singular thought not be opaque to general reasoning; with the quantificational apparatus understood, the step from the accessible general form Fx to its universal closure is a step within the same inferential competence that Evans requires for thinking of a at all. So understanding Fa together with understanding ‘∀’ puts ∀x Fx within your grasp.

1.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the possessability of a mode of presentation, not on what you believe under that mode of presentation.

If you are able to think the singular thought that a is F, i.e. you have a mode of presentation M under which you think of a as F, Evans requires that M be a mode of presentation which you can employ in general. In particular M must be such that you are able to think thoughts of the form

    M(b) ,  i.e.  F(x)

with the same constituent F and an arbitrary free variable in place of the singular term. That is what it is to possess the concept F in a generalizable way. Possessing F in that way is what makes the thought Fa thinkable at all.

The open schema F(x) is thereby licensed, and if you in addition possess an understanding of universal quantification you can parse the closed sentence ∀x Fx. The Generality Constraint does not however require you to think, believe or even understand the truth conditions of that closed generalisation. The closed universal ∀x Fx is a particular propositional content with a truth value, and its intelligibility is the conjunction of an intelligible predicate F, an intelligible quantifier ∀, and a disposition to evaluate the universal claim. The constraint only gives you the first two items, the generalizable mode of presentation F(x).

In other words Evans gives you the variable form F(x) and hence the capacity to think about F in general, not a commitment to the universal proposition ∀x Fx. You can understand the schema F(x), and with an understanding of ∀ you can understand the syntax of ∀x Fx, but understanding Fa does not by itself force you to understand, let alone accept, that everything is F. That is why the classic Egocentric and demonstration examples can be ruled out: they lack a generalizable mode of presentation, not because the subject cannot be made to utter a universally quantified sentence.

9.text:
The generality constraint is a constraint on thinkability and not on truth. 
Evans states it for singular thoughts in something like the following form:

If an agent can entertain a thought that contains a particular object a in a certain mode of presentation F, then she must be able to entertain the same mode of presentation F apart from the particularity of a, i.e. she must be able to entertain the open sentence

   Fx

with a free variable x, so that she can think of a as a value of the variable in the scheme Fx. That is what it is to be able to think of a as an instance of a general concept F.

It is not a license to universalise. The open schema Fx is generalizable in the sense that it can be applied to a variable, it is not the closed sentence

   ∀x Fx

which says that F holds of every object in the domain. To be able to entertain ∀x Fx a thinker has to be able to entertain F as true of every x, which is a very much stronger epistemic and conceptual requirement than being able to entertain F of a variable.

Hence what the constraint guarantees from an understanding of Fa is at most an understanding of the open formula Fx, i.e. the ability to think of F as a property that can be attributed to an arbitrary x of which a is a particular instance. It does not by itself guarantee an understanding of the universal closure ∀x Fx. Even granted for the sake of argument that the agent understands the universal quantifier in the abstract, syntactic combinability of an understood predicate Fx with an understood quantifier is not semantic understanding of the universal generalisation. The generalisation from Fa to ∀x Fx is a substantive inference, and a failure to be able to make it is exactly the phenomenon Evans discusses with sortal restricted domains and with concepts that are not fully generalizable.

In the ordinary rendering the constraint is therefore often expressed as the requirement to understand Fx with a free variable, not to understand ∀x Fx. The latter is generalizability plus universal quantification.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On the Evansian picture the mode of presentation you deploy in thinking that a is F is not an idiosyncratic, Fa-bound package. To understand Fa at all you must grasp F as a genuinely general predicate concept and you must grasp a under a mode of presentation that is available for iteration.

The Generality Constraint is the demand for systematicity: a way of thinking of an object that can figure in one thought Fa can figure in thoughts with any other conceptually expressible predicate. Once F is understood as a concept with a uniform application condition, that understanding is not essentially indexed to a. And since you are assumed to understand universal quantification, you have the logical resources to move from a particular application of F to the general application of F.

In other words, if your grasp of F were essentially tied to the particular a, so that you could affirm Fa but you could not even entertain ∀x Fx, your grasp of F would be defective in precisely the way the Generality Constraint rules out. Understanding Fa therefore presupposes an understanding of F in the general form Fx which, with a grasp of the universal quantifier, is just understanding ∀x Fx.

8.text:
Gareth Evans' Generality Constraint is a constraint on modes of presentation, not on 
truth conditions. What the Constraint says is that the possession of the singular
thought that a is F must involve the possession of the general concept F as a
concept which can be applied to an arbitrary object. If a thinker can think of a
under the concept F the thinker must be able to think of F in a way which is
not essentially tied to the particular object a, i.e. he must be in possession
of the open proposition schema

Fx

and the capacity to instantiate it with an arbitrary object. In that sense
you cannot understand Fa in virtue of a purely a-indexed mode of presentation
of F; you must be able to entertain F of a variable.

That generalizability is not the same thing as being able to understand, let
alone believe, the universal closure

∀x Fx

as a substantive claim about the world. The universal closure is the claim
that everything is F. It is a perfectly distinct proposition from Fa. The
fact that you have the general concept F in virtue of understanding Fa and
that, ex hypothesi, you understand the operator ∀, is of course enough for
you to parse the syntactic string ∀x Fx and to know what it would mean if it
were true. What the Generality Constraint does not give you is any content
about the extension of F, and in particular it does not entail that from the
understanding of the particular Fa you understand, or should be in a position
to understand, the universal generalisation that all x are F. The constraint
only requires the ability to think about F in the general form Fx and, more
precisely in Evans' own formulation, to think about a via the general
thought ∀x[x=a → Fx]. The universal claim ∀x Fx is a further, substantive
thought about the world which goes well beyond the content of Fa. 

That is the usual reason for the negative Evansian argument against
irreducibly singular, non-generalizable thoughts: you can have Fa only if you
have F as a general concept, and you have F as a general concept only if you
can think of it with a variable, not because you are committed to the truth of
the universal generalisation of it.

10.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on conceptual competence not on
truth value.

If you can think a singular thought expressed as *Fa* you have to possess the
concept *F* and deploy it in thinking of a. Evans' point is that the mode
of presentation of the property in such a thought has to be a mode that is
available for systematic redeployment. In particular a concept that can be
used in the singular thought *Fa* has to be available for use with a
variable and for systematic substitution of the singular term. That is what
it is to grasp *F* as a concept at all.

On that picture to understand *Fa* is already to understand *F* as a
predicate that can be applied to *a* and, by the same token, to *b*, to *x*,
etc. The open schema *Fx* is therefore intelligible to you, and the schema
is the material you need to form the closed quantificational thought
*∀x Fx*.

So far as intelligibility goes, and on the stated assumption that you do
already understand universal quantification, the universal closure of the
schema is intelligible to you. Evans does not require you to know that
*∀x Fx* is true, nor to know the extension of *F*; he requires only that the
thought you are said to entertain be one you could in principle redeploy
with a variable and, given a grasp of the quantifier, close under that
variable. That is the minimal generality that makes *Fa* a thinkable
thought at all.

The constraint is therefore normally read as requiring that an
understanding of *Fa* entails an understanding of the general form *Fx*
and hence, once quantification is itself understood, an understanding of
the universal generalisation *∀x Fx*. Knowing its truth is another matter.

15.text:
Under Evans the grasp of a singular thought is parasitic on the possession
of the general concept that is expressed in it.

To think that a is F is to think of a under the mode of presentation F.
If F were only ever available to you as *that*-property-of-a you could not
think of a as F at all, for then you would have no way of telling F off
against any other property and no way of telling what it is that you are
attributing to a. The GC is the requirement that the mode of presentation
which figures in a singular thought be a genuinely general way of thinking
of objects, i.e. that it be available for the thinking of other objects as
well.

Hence if you can think the singular thought Fa you already possess the
general concept F. Possession of the concept F is possession of the open
schema Fx, the ability to entertain ‘x is F’ for an arbitrary object x and
to go through substitution instances of it. That is what it is for F to be
general.

Given that, and given by hypothesis a grasp of the quantifier ∀, you can
make syntactic and semantic sense of the closed sentence ∀x Fx. You will
be able to entertain the general thought ‘x is F’, and, with the quantifier
in your repertoire, the universal generalisation of it. What the GC does
not give you is the truth of ∀x Fx or even the belief that it is true.
Fa does not entail ∀x Fx. The constraint is a constraint on the
possession conditions for the concept F that figures in Fa, not a
material entailment from a singular instance to the universal claim.
In the usual loose formulation this is expressed as: to understand Fa
you must be able to understand Fx for an arbitrary x, and with a grasp of
∀ that is the ability to understand the universal generalisation ∀x Fx.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, not in the sense that Evans requires you to be able to grasp, or
even to be committed to, the truth of the universal generalisation ∀xFx.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the form of a way of thinking,
not a commitment to a substantive general truth about the domain.  If S can
think the singular thought that a is F, then S must be able to think of a
under a mode of presentation that is generalizable.  In particular S must
be able to think of a as the value of a variable and to think of F as a
property that can be ascribed to an object under that variable, i.e. S must
have the open schema ‘x is F’ and be able to think of a as a possible
instantiation of x.  That is the generalizability required by the
Constraint.

Understanding the open schema ‘Fx’ and being able to deploy the predicate
F in general thoughts about objects in the domain is what the Constraint
secures.  It does not secure an understanding of, or a belief in, the
specific proposition ∀xFx, that everything in the domain is F.  Grasping
∀xFx is a further, substantive semantic and epistemic commitment: it is
the claim that F holds of every object one can quantify over. Understanding
‘Fa’ together with a competent grasp of the quantifier ‘∀’ at most gives
you the syntactic capacity to form the sentence ∀xFx. It does not give you
contentful understanding of that universal claim, nor does Evans require it.
One can perfectly well understand that a particular a is F, and be able to
think of F in general as in ‘x is F’, while having no information whatever
about whether F holds of b, c, … and while therefore not understanding, in
the contentful sense, the proposition ∀xFx. The Constraint demands
generalizability of the mode of presentation of F and of a, not universal
instantiation of F.

2.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on concept possession, not a constraint
on what you know or what you believe about the distribution of a property.

To think that a is F in Evans' sense is to possess the concept F in a way which
can be combined with a mode of presentation of a. Possession of F in this way
is possession of it as a Fregean unsaturated component. If F is so possessed
then the thinker can entertain the same component F combined with any
appropriate object variable. In Evans' words the character of a thought is
such that if you can think of one thing in that way you must be able to think
of another thing in the same way. You must be able to entertain the schema

    x is F

with x free and to apply it to any object you are in a position to refer to.
That is the schematic generality that is required for there to be a
rule-governed use of the predicate F at all.

It is not the generality of the closed universal proposition

    ∀x Fx

as a truth evaluable claim about every object in the domain. From the
possession of the concept F which underlies the understanding of Fa you get
the ability to understand the open sentence Fx and, having mastered the
syntax and semantics of the universal quantifier, to understand the
syntactic form ∀x Fx. You do not get a guarantee that you can evaluate
∀x Fx, nor that it is true, nor even that you can coherently entertain it
as a substantive belief about a. All that Fa gives you is the particular
instantiation F[a/x]; the constraint only guarantees that you have F
available for instantiation, not that every instantiation holds. In the
usual loose way of speaking this is described as `being able to understand
Fx in general', i.e. being able to think Fx with x as a variable. It is
that schematic ability, and not the ability to understand and know the
particular closed proposition ∀x Fx, that the Generality Constraint
requires.

11.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on modes of presentation, not on what you happen to believe about the extension of F.

To understand and think that a is F in the Evansian sense is to think of a under the concept F. That is only possible at all if F is a concept which you possess as a general concept, i.e. a concept which is deployable in thought of the form `... is F ...` for arbitrary arguments.  In Evans’ words, a thinker who can think the singular thought Fa must be able to think of the very same way of thinking of a as F in a way which is not essentially tied to a. He must be able to entertain the schema

   F x

and to substitute for x any individual the thinker can refer to, and therefore he must possess the general concept F.

That is a requirement on conceptual competence with the predicate F. It is not a requirement that you can, or must, make the substantive general claim

   ∀x Fx

on the basis of being able to think Fa.  Having the general concept F and having a grasp of the universal quantifier is of course enough for you to be syntactically competent with the closed sentence ∀x Fx and to know what it would mean for it to be true, but Fa gives you no reason to think it is true, and Evans does not claim that the ability to think one instance of F is the same as the ability to assert the universal generalisation of F.  The constraint gives you the open schema Fx, i.e. the ability to think of F in general and to think of any a′ as Fa′, not an entailment from Fa to ∀x Fx.

If Fx is read simply as the general schema ‘x is F’ the constraint says yes, you must be able to deploy F generally. That is all that is required for singular understanding on Evans’ view. The closed universal proposition ∀x Fx is a further, substantive claim about the extension of F which is not forced by the Generality Constraint and is not in general justified by the possession of the singular thought Fa.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans’ formulation the Generality Constraint is a requirement on the mode of presentation in which a singular term is grasped. To understand a thought of the form Fa you must be able to think of the object a under the general concept F, and that in turn requires that F be available to you as a genuinely general, iterable concept.

If F is genuinely general you must be able to entertain the schema Fx for a variable x, i.e. you must be able to think of F as applicable in the open form. That is just the requirement that the concept F be accessible independently of a particular instantiation. 

Given that for the sake of argument you do understand universal quantification, entertaining the open schema Fx gives you the resources to close it. The universal closure ∀x Fx is then the natural general expression of the same concept F that you were already using in Fa. So understanding Fa commits you, via generality, to understanding the general form Fx, and with a grasp of ∀ you can move from the general form Fx to the closed universal proposition ∀x Fx. That is exactly what the constraint is meant to secure: understanding a singular instance entails understanding the generality of the concept involved.

12.text:
The generality constraint is a constraint on what it is to have a mode of presentation of an object at all. To think of a particular a, on Evans’ picture, is to think of a under some concept F that is possessed in a form that is in principle substitutable for other objects.

If S thinks, or understands, that a is F then S cannot be thinking of a with a primitive, unrepeatable singular mode of presentation. The mode of presentation that makes the thought about a possible is the general concept F. Possessing F as a mode of presentation of a just is possessing F as a property that can be thought of as applying to any item in the domain. In logical terms you must have the open sentence schema Fx in your repertoire and be able to apply it to items of the domain one by one.

Hence understanding the singular token proposition Fa presupposes understanding the schema Fx, i.e. the ability to think of an arbitrary x as F, and to substitute co-referential singular terms in the thought without loss of content. That is the generality of the thought.

Given that possession of the quantifier ∀ is presupposed, possession of the open schema Fx entails possession of the closed form ∀x Fx. Understanding Fa therefore entails in principle understanding the general form Fx and, with a grasp of universal quantification, the closed generalization ∀x Fx. Understanding the form is of course not the same as endorsing or knowing the truth of ∀x Fx; you can perfectly well understand ∀x Fx while believing ¬∀x Fx, e.g. believing Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx. The constraint is conceptual, not doxastic: the singular instance is parasitic on the general concept.

4.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the mode of presentation of the
object a in the singular thought Fa, not a constraint on the extension of F.

If S can think Fa in a singular way at all then S must think of a under a
mode of presentation which is itself generalizable.  In Evans’ terms S must
be able to think of a under a concept that can be used in reasoning and in
forming general thoughts about a.  That is the requirement that the singular
thought be possible only on the basis of a mastery of F as a general
concept: S must be able to entertain the open sentence Fx and in the
canonical form to entertain

     ∀x [x = a → Fx]

i.e. the thought that a is F thought of in a way that is substitutable
for a variable bound by the same concept F. The thought is then
generalizable over the subject term a, not over the predicate F.

Understanding Fa plus understanding the quantifier ∀ of course gives you the
syntactic competence to parse the sentence ∀x Fx, but the Generality
Constraint does not require you to entertain, and in particular does not
require you to be justified in entertaining, the unrestricted universal
claim that everything is F.  ∀x Fx is strictly stronger than Fa and may be
false, unknown to S and in any case is not the generalization of Fa over a.
What the constraint requires is generalizability of the singular mode of
presentation of a, e.g. the ability to think of a as the filler of F and to
reason with Fx as an open formula, not the ability to understand or to
accept the strong universal proposition ∀x Fx.  Understanding Fa therefore
does not by itself give you understanding of ∀x Fx in the substantive Evansian
sense.

In other words, if your grasp of F were essentially tied to the particular a, so that you could affirm Fa but you could not even entertain ∀x Fx, your grasp of F would be defective in precisely the way the Generality Constraint rules out. Understanding Fa therefore presupposes an understanding of F in the general form Fx which, with a grasp of the universal quantifier, is just understanding ∀x Fx.

Gareth Evans' Generality Constraint is a constraint on modes of presentation, not on 
truth conditions. What the Constraint says is that the possession of the singular
thought that a is F must involve the possession of the general concept F as a
concept which can be applied to an arbitrary object. If a thinker can think of a
under the concept F the thinker must be able to think of F in a way which is
not essentially tied to the particular object a, i.e. he must be in possession
of the open proposition schema

Fx

and the capacity to instantiate it with an arbitrary object. In that sense
you cannot understand Fa in virtue of a purely a-indexed mode of presentation
of F; you must be able to entertain F of a variable.

That generalizability is not the same thing as being able to understand, let
alone believe, the universal closure

∀x Fx

as a substantive claim about the world. The universal closure is the claim
that everything is F. It is a perfectly distinct proposition from Fa. The
fact that you have the general concept F in virtue of understanding Fa and
that, ex hypothesi, you understand the operator ∀, is of course enough for
you to parse the syntactic string ∀x Fx and to know what it would mean if it
were true. What the Generality Constraint does not give you is any content
about the extension of F, and in particular it does not entail that from the
understanding of the particular Fa you understand, or should be in a position
to understand, the universal generalisation that all x are F. The constraint
only requires the ability to think about F in the general form Fx and, more
precisely in Evans' own formulation, to think about a via the general
thought ∀x[x=a → Fx]. The universal claim ∀x Fx is a further, substantive
thought about the world which goes well beyond the content of Fa. 

That is the usual reason for the negative Evansian argument against
irreducibly singular, non-generalizable thoughts: you can have Fa only if you
have F as a general concept, and you have F as a general concept only if you
can think of it with a variable, not because you are committed to the truth of
the universal generalisation of it.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on conceptual competence not on
truth value.

If you can think a singular thought expressed as *Fa* you have to possess the
concept *F* and deploy it in thinking of a. Evans' point is that the mode
of presentation of the property in such a thought has to be a mode that is
available for systematic redeployment. In particular a concept that can be
used in the singular thought *Fa* has to be available for use with a
variable and for systematic substitution of the singular term. That is what
it is to grasp *F* as a concept at all.

On that picture to understand *Fa* is already to understand *F* as a
predicate that can be applied to *a* and, by the same token, to *b*, to *x*,
etc. The open schema *Fx* is therefore intelligible to you, and the schema
is the material you need to form the closed quantificational thought
*∀x Fx*.

So far as intelligibility goes, and on the stated assumption that you do
already understand universal quantification, the universal closure of the
schema is intelligible to you. Evans does not require you to know that
*∀x Fx* is true, nor to know the extension of *F*; he requires only that the
thought you are said to entertain be one you could in principle redeploy
with a variable and, given a grasp of the quantifier, close under that
variable. That is the minimal generality that makes *Fa* a thinkable
thought at all.

The constraint is therefore normally read as requiring that an
understanding of *Fa* entails an understanding of the general form *Fx*
and hence, once quantification is itself understood, an understanding of
the universal generalisation *∀x Fx*. Knowing its truth is another matter.

Under Evans the grasp of a singular thought is parasitic on the possession
of the general concept that is expressed in it.

To think that a is F is to think of a under the mode of presentation F.
If F were only ever available to you as *that*-property-of-a you could not
think of a as F at all, for then you would have no way of telling F off
against any other property and no way of telling what it is that you are
attributing to a. The GC is the requirement that the mode of presentation
which figures in a singular thought be a genuinely general way of thinking
of objects, i.e. that it be available for the thinking of other objects as
well.

Hence if you can think the singular thought Fa you already possess the
general concept F. Possession of the concept F is possession of the open
schema Fx, the ability to entertain ‘x is F’ for an arbitrary object x and
to go through substitution instances of it. That is what it is for F to be
general.

Given that, and given by hypothesis a grasp of the quantifier ∀, you can
make syntactic and semantic sense of the closed sentence ∀x Fx. You will
be able to entertain the general thought ‘x is F’, and, with the quantifier
in your repertoire, the universal generalisation of it. What the GC does
not give you is the truth of ∀x Fx or even the belief that it is true.
Fa does not entail ∀x Fx. The constraint is a constraint on the
possession conditions for the concept F that figures in Fa, not a
material entailment from a singular instance to the universal claim.
In the usual loose formulation this is expressed as: to understand Fa
you must be able to understand Fx for an arbitrary x, and with a grasp of
∀ that is the ability to understand the universal generalisation ∀x Fx.

even to be committed to, the truth of the universal generalisation ∀xFx.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the form of a way of thinking,
not a commitment to a substantive general truth about the domain.  If S can
think the singular thought that a is F, then S must be able to think of a
under a mode of presentation that is generalizable.  In particular S must
be able to think of a as the value of a variable and to think of F as a
property that can be ascribed to an object under that variable, i.e. S must
have the open schema ‘x is F’ and be able to think of a as a possible
instantiation of x.  That is the generalizability required by the
Constraint.

Understanding the open schema ‘Fx’ and being able to deploy the predicate
F in general thoughts about objects in the domain is what the Constraint
secures.  It does not secure an understanding of, or a belief in, the
specific proposition ∀xFx, that everything in the domain is F.  Grasping
∀xFx is a further, substantive semantic and epistemic commitment: it is
the claim that F holds of every object one can quantify over. Understanding
‘Fa’ together with a competent grasp of the quantifier ‘∀’ at most gives
you the syntactic capacity to form the sentence ∀xFx. It does not give you
contentful understanding of that universal claim, nor does Evans require it.
One can perfectly well understand that a particular a is F, and be able to
think of F in general as in ‘x is F’, while having no information whatever
about whether F holds of b, c, … and while therefore not understanding, in
the contentful sense, the proposition ∀xFx. The Constraint demands
generalizability of the mode of presentation of F and of a, not universal
instantiation of F.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on concept possession, not a constraint
on what you know or what you believe about the distribution of a property.

To think that a is F in Evans' sense is to possess the concept F in a way which
can be combined with a mode of presentation of a. Possession of F in this way
is possession of it as a Fregean unsaturated component. If F is so possessed
then the thinker can entertain the same component F combined with any
appropriate object variable. In Evans' words the character of a thought is
such that if you can think of one thing in that way you must be able to think
of another thing in the same way. You must be able to entertain the schema

    x is F

with x free and to apply it to any object you are in a position to refer to.
That is the schematic generality that is required for there to be a
rule-governed use of the predicate F at all.

It is not the generality of the closed universal proposition

    ∀x Fx

as a truth evaluable claim about every object in the domain. From the
possession of the concept F which underlies the understanding of Fa you get
the ability to understand the open sentence Fx and, having mastered the
syntax and semantics of the universal quantifier, to understand the
syntactic form ∀x Fx. You do not get a guarantee that you can evaluate
∀x Fx, nor that it is true, nor even that you can coherently entertain it
as a substantive belief about a. All that Fa gives you is the particular
instantiation F[a/x]; the constraint only guarantees that you have F
available for instantiation, not that every instantiation holds. In the
usual loose way of speaking this is described as `being able to understand
Fx in general', i.e. being able to think Fx with x as a variable. It is
that schematic ability, and not the ability to understand and know the
particular closed proposition ∀x Fx, that the Generality Constraint
requires.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on modes of presentation, not on what you happen to believe about the extension of F.

To understand and think that a is F in the Evansian sense is to think of a under the concept F. That is only possible at all if F is a concept which you possess as a general concept, i.e. a concept which is deployable in thought of the form `... is F ...` for arbitrary arguments.  In Evans’ words, a thinker who can think the singular thought Fa must be able to think of the very same way of thinking of a as F in a way which is not essentially tied to a. He must be able to entertain the schema

   F x

and to substitute for x any individual the thinker can refer to, and therefore he must possess the general concept F.

That is a requirement on conceptual competence with the predicate F. It is not a requirement that you can, or must, make the substantive general claim

   ∀x Fx

on the basis of being able to think Fa.  Having the general concept F and having a grasp of the universal quantifier is of course enough for you to be syntactically competent with the closed sentence ∀x Fx and to know what it would mean for it to be true, but Fa gives you no reason to think it is true, and Evans does not claim that the ability to think one instance of F is the same as the ability to assert the universal generalisation of F.  The constraint gives you the open schema Fx, i.e. the ability to think of F in general and to think of any a′ as Fa′, not an entailment from Fa to ∀x Fx.

If Fx is read simply as the general schema ‘x is F’ the constraint says yes, you must be able to deploy F generally. That is all that is required for singular understanding on Evans’ view. The closed universal proposition ∀x Fx is a further, substantive claim about the extension of F which is not forced by the Generality Constraint and is not in general justified by the possession of the singular thought Fa.

The generality constraint is a constraint on what it is to have a mode of presentation of an object at all. To think of a particular a, on Evans’ picture, is to think of a under some concept F that is possessed in a form that is in principle substitutable for other objects.

If S thinks, or understands, that a is F then S cannot be thinking of a with a primitive, unrepeatable singular mode of presentation. The mode of presentation that makes the thought about a possible is the general concept F. Possessing F as a mode of presentation of a just is possessing F as a property that can be thought of as applying to any item in the domain. In logical terms you must have the open sentence schema Fx in your repertoire and be able to apply it to items of the domain one by one.

Hence understanding the singular token proposition Fa presupposes understanding the schema Fx, i.e. the ability to think of an arbitrary x as F, and to substitute co-referential singular terms in the thought without loss of content. That is the generality of the thought.

Given that possession of the quantifier ∀ is presupposed, possession of the open schema Fx entails possession of the closed form ∀x Fx. Understanding Fa therefore entails in principle understanding the general form Fx and, with a grasp of universal quantification, the closed generalization ∀x Fx. Understanding the form is of course not the same as endorsing or knowing the truth of ∀x Fx; you can perfectly well understand ∀x Fx while believing ¬∀x Fx, e.g. believing Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx. The constraint is conceptual, not doxastic: the singular instance is parasitic on the general concept.
public_text.4:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the mode of presentation of the
object a in the singular thought Fa, not a constraint on the extension of F.

If S can think Fa in a singular way at all then S must think of a under a
mode of presentation which is itself generalizable.  In Evans’ terms S must
be able to think of a under a concept that can be used in reasoning and in
forming general thoughts about a.  That is the requirement that the singular
thought be possible only on the basis of a mastery of F as a general
concept: S must be able to entertain the open sentence Fx and in the
canonical form to entertain

     ∀x [x = a → Fx]

i.e. the thought that a is F thought of in a way that is substitutable
for a variable bound by the same concept F. The thought is then
generalizable over the subject term a, not over the predicate F.

Understanding Fa plus understanding the quantifier ∀ of course gives you the
syntactic competence to parse the sentence ∀x Fx, but the Generality
Constraint does not require you to entertain, and in particular does not
require you to be justified in entertaining, the unrestricted universal
claim that everything is F.  ∀x Fx is strictly stronger than Fa and may be
false, unknown to S and in any case is not the generalization of Fa over a.
What the constraint requires is generalizability of the singular mode of
presentation of a, e.g. the ability to think of a as the filler of F and to
reason with Fx as an open formula, not the ability to understand or to
accept the strong universal proposition ∀x Fx.  Understanding Fa therefore
does not by itself give you understanding of ∀x Fx in the substantive Evansian
sense.

Core Evansian point agreed on: to think Fa at all you must possess F as a genuinely general, iterable concept. The mode of presentation used in Fa cannot be a-indexed or idiosyncratic; it must be available for redeployment with other arguments. That gives:

* possession of the open schema Fx, i.e. the ability to think ‘x is F’ with a free variable and to substitute arbitrary singular terms for x;
* generalizability of the concept F and, in Evans’ formulation, generalizability of the mode of presentation of a, e.g. the ability to think ∀x[x=a → Fx].

Disagreement is about the step from the open schema to the closed universal ∀x Fx, given the stipulation that universal quantification is already understood.

Yes-side: 10,12,13,14,3,7 hold that grasp of F as general + a grasp of ∀ gives intelligibility of the universal closure. On this reading understanding Fa already commits you to F(x) and, with quantifier competence, to being able to understand/undertake the closed generalisation ∀x Fx. 15 and 5 make the same syntactic point but stress it is only capacity to make sense of the sentence, not truth or belief.

No/nuanced-side: 1,2,4,6,8,9 hold that Generality is a constraint on conceptual competence/mode of presentation, not on truth value or doxastic commitment. The constraint secures the open form Fx, not the substantive proposition ∀x Fx that everything is F. Syntactic combinability of an understood predicate with an understood quantifier is not the same as contentful understanding of the universal claim, and Evans does not require you to know, believe or even entertain the truth conditions of ∀x Fx. Fa gives no warrant for ∀x Fx, and one can understand Fa and Fx while believing ¬∀x Fx.

a) syntactic/semantic parsability given quantifier competence, which follows from the open schema, or
b) contentful grasp / entitlement to the universal proposition, which Generality alone does not give.

reflection_text.2:

Consensus across colleagues:

* No / nuanced camp: Colleagues 1,2,4,6,8,9,11 emphasize a distinction between schematic generalizability and substantive universal content. The GC gives you the open form Fx, not an entailment to the closed proposition ∀x Fx. Understanding the quantifier syntactically lets you parse ∀x Fx, but Evans does not require contentful understanding, evaluation, or endorsement of the universal claim ‘everything is F’. The closed universal is a distinct proposition with its own truth conditions and is not forced by Fa; you can understand Fa and Fx while believing ¬∀x Fx, e.g. Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx.

Key unresolved tension in my own view: whether ‘understand ∀x Fx’ is meant as syntactic/semantic intelligibility given an open schema + quantifier competence, or as contentful grasp/evaluability of the universal claim. Evans’ own formulation is often rendered as generalizability to the free-variable schema, and the requirement for the closed universal is typically presented as generality plus independent quantificational competence, not as a direct consequence of Fa alone. The constraint rules out a purely a-indexed mode of presentation and explains egocentric/demonstration cases, not a commitment to universal instantiation.

I retain the core distinction: GC → open schema Fx is necessary for Fa; universal closure ∀x Fx is intelligible in virtue of schema + quantifier grasp, but it is not a doxastic or epistemic requirement of GC and Fa does not entail its truth.

2.text:
The Generality Constraint is a condition on concept possession, not on belief.

To think or understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to think of a under the concept F. F can figure in that thought only if it is possessed as a genuinely unsaturated, general concept. That is the requirement that the mode of presentation you use for a in Fa be available for redeployment with other arguments. In particular you must possess the open schema

Fx

with a free variable, and the ability to substitute arbitrary singular terms you can refer to for x. Possession of Fa is parasitic on possession of F in that generalizable form. That is what the GC secures.

That generalizability does not by itself give you a substantive commitment to the extension of F. From possession of F and of a suitable grasp of the quantifier you do get syntactic/semantic intelligibility of the closed form

∀x Fx

once ∀ is understood. Given Fx as an open schema and a grasp of ∀ you can form the universal closure, see what would make it true and what would make it false, and you can entertain it as a proposition. The closed universal is the natural closure of the very general concept you are already committed to by Fa.

It is not a doxastic or epistemic requirement of the GC, and Fa does not entail ∀x Fx. The constraint gives you the general concept F and hence the open form Fx, and with independent quantificational competence the intelligibility of the universal closure. It does not require you to believe, know or be able to evaluate ∀x Fx as true. You can perfectly understand Fa and Fx, understand ∀, and yet believe ¬∀x Fx, e.g. Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx.

So understanding Fa commits you to F as a general concept, to the schema Fx, and, on the stipulated assumption that you understand universal quantification, to the intelligibility of ∀x Fx as the universal closure of that schema. The commitment is conceptual / schematic, not a material entailment to the truth of the universal generalisation.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I want to push back on the open/closed split that 1, 11, 8 and 2 are drawing. They are right that the Generality Constraint gives you the open schema Fx and a generalizable mode of presentation of F, and that GC is not a commitment to the truth of ∀x Fx. That much is uncontroversial.

Where I think they go wrong is in turning that into a claim that you do not understand the closed form once you already understand the quantifier. The competence they grant is exactly what is needed for understanding ∀x Fx.

If you understand Fa on Evans' account you must possess F as a general concept, i.e. you must be able to entertain Fx for an arbitrary x and to substitute co-referentially in that schema. Possession of the quantifier by hypothesis gives you the further competence to close that schema. Understanding ∀ is understanding the function from an open schema to its closure and what it would be for that closure to be true/false.

So the move from Fx to ∀x Fx is not a substantive doxastic commitment, it is a purely conceptual one. As 15 puts it, you can make syntactic and semantic sense of the closed sentence, and as 10, 12 and 13 note, the singular instance is parasitic on the general concept. Once F is general and ∀ is understood, the universal generalisation is intelligible to you in the same sense in which Fx is intelligible: you can tell what would make it true and what would make it false, even if you believe it is false.

The No position ends up saying you can understand the schema and you can understand the quantifier, but you cannot understand their combination. That is an odd way to define understanding. Evans requires generalizability precisely so that thoughts are not opaque to quantification. To be able to think Fa is to be able to think F in the form Fx, and with a grasp of ∀ that is just to be able to think ∀x Fx. Understanding the universal is not endorsing it.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the pressure is toward Yes once we grant quantifier competence, and the No replies are conflating understanding a proposition with believing or knowing it to be true.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on possession of a mode of presentation, not on doxastic commitment. If you can think the singular thought Fa, you cannot be thinking of a under a mode of presentation that is essentially indexed to a. You must possess F as a genuinely general, iterable concept. That is what it is to possess F at all on Evans’ picture: possession of F just is possession of the open form Fx and the capacity to apply it with variable substitution.

That is not a further optional fact about F, it is the condition for Fa to be thinkable. The schema Fx is the general way of thinking of objects as F that makes the singular instance Fa possible. Now the question adds by hypothesis that the subject understands universal quantification. Understanding ∀ is understanding the operation that takes an open schema and forms the closed general claim. Given Fx is already intelligible to you as the general mode in which F is possessed, and given you understand ∀, what more is needed for ∀x Fx to be intelligible? You already know what it is for x to be F, and you know what ∀x means.

Colleagues 1, 11, 2, 8, 9 point out correctly that GC does not require you to believe ∀x Fx or to know its extension. That is true, and it is true for Fa as well. I think the No side is conflating understanding a universal proposition with believing it true or being able to evaluate it, and that’s not what Evans is asking for.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on possession conditions for a concept, not on doxastic commitment to the extension of that concept. If you can think the singular thought Fa, Evans requires that the mode of presentation of F that you deploy in Fa be a mode you can deploy independently of a. That is possession of F as a general, iterable concept, i.e. possession of the open schema Fx. You cannot have a genuinely singular, a-indexed grasp of F and still count as thinking Fa in Evans’ sense.

That is already agreed on by the No camp: Fa entails an ability to think Fx with a free variable, to substitute co-referential singular terms, to deploy F systematically. If you already have that schematic competence, and by hypothesis you understand universal quantification, then you have the material for the universal closure. Understanding ∀ is not a mysterious extra power; it is the ability to make sense of taking an open schema and closing it under a quantifier. 

On that minimal semantic notion of understanding – being able to grasp what the expression means, what would make it true and what would make it false – possession of the general concept F together with possession of ∀ is possession of the intelligibility of ∀x Fx. You can perfectly well understand ∀x Fx while thinking ¬∀x Fx, e.g. believing Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx. Understanding is not endorsement.

To deny that Fa yields understanding of ∀x Fx is therefore to deny that the open schema Fx is genuinely general. It would be to allow a mode of presentation of F that is available for substitution only in the limited, non-quantificational sense of “I can apply F to b too”, but which is somehow opaque to quantificational closure. That is exactly the kind of non-generalizable mode Evans rules out. Evans talks of being able to think ∀x[x=a → Fx] rather than Fa, i.e. of a generalizable way of thinking of a under F. The universal operator is built into that generalizability.

So with grasp of ∀ assumed, understanding Fa is understanding F as general, and understanding F as general is understanding its universal closure. The constraint does not require you to know that ∀x Fx is true, and it does not give you warrant to believe it, only that the concept you deploy in Fa is available under the quantifier. That is the sense in which understanding Fa entails understanding ∀x Fx.

   Fx  /  ‘x is F’

with x free for substitution and you can entertain F of an arbitrary object you can refer to. That redeployability is what makes a singular thought Fa thinkable at all. In particular you must be able to think the canonical Evansian generalisation

   ∀x [x = a → Fx]

which is the generalizability of the mode of presentation of a under F.

That is already the generality that the GC licenses. It is a conceptual competence with the predicate F, and it is doxastic-neutral. It does not license the material inference Fa → ∀x Fx, nor does it commit you to the truth, knowledge or even belief that ∀x Fx.

reflection_text.1:
The discussion is stable around a core consensus and a persistent split over how far the consensus extends to the closed universal.

Common ground retained from earlier rounds and reinforced in round 1:
* GC is a possession / mode-of-presentation condition on conceptual competence, not a truth, belief or doxastic condition.
* To think/understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to think of a under a genuinely general, iterable concept F. Possession of F is possession of the unsaturated component F, i.e. the open schematic form Fx / ‘x is F’ with free variable and systematic substitutability for singular terms. That schematic generalizability is what makes the singular thought thinkable at all.
* Evans’ canonical statement of the required generalizability is of the singular mode of presentation of a, e.g. the ability to entertain ∀x[x = a → Fx], not the unrestricted predicate universalisation ∀x Fx. The constraint rules out a-indexed, egocentric/demonstrative, non-redeployable modes of presentation.

Disagreement in round 1 is about the status of the closed universal ∀x Fx given the stipulation that universal quantification is already understood.

Thin-intelligibility / Yes-in-the-formal-sense position, held in various shades by colleagues 10,12,13,14,15,2,6,7:
* Fa requires the general concept F, i.e. the open schema Fx. With an independent grasp of ∀ the resources to close the schema are present. Possession of an intelligible predicate Fx plus an intelligible quantifier ∀ is enough for compositional / syntactic-semantic intelligibility of the string ∀x Fx: one can see what would make the closure true/false and entertain it as a proposition.
* In the loose Evansian way of speaking this is expressed as: understanding Fa entails understanding the general form Fx and, once ∀ is understood, understanding the universal generalisation ∀x Fx in the sense of being able to make sense of it / parse it. The constraint does not make you believe or know ∀x Fx true, nor does it give epistemic warrant for it.

Schematic-only / No-to-substantive-commitment position, held by colleagues 1,11,4,5,8,9,3:
* GC gives you the open schema Fx and the generalizability of the mode of presentation of a. It does not give you a substantive commitment to, or contentful understanding/evaluability of, the closed proposition ∀x Fx that everything is F.
* Syntactic combinability of an understood predicate Fx with an understood quantifier is not semantic/contentful understanding of the universal claim about the extension of F. The move from the intelligible schema to the substantive universal proposition is a material inference about the world, not a conceptual requirement for thinkability of Fa. One can understand Fa, understand Fx schematically, understand ∀, and still believe ¬∀x Fx, e.g. Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx.

Push-back in round 1:
* Colleagues 13,14,7 argue the thin/substantive split collapses once quantifier competence is granted. Possession of F as general just is possession of Fx; understanding ∀ is understanding closure of schemas. To be able to think Fa is to be able to think F in the form Fx, and with ∀ understood that is just to be able to think ∀x Fx. A defective grasp of F would be one where you could affirm Fa but could not even entertain ∀x Fx – exactly the defect GC rules out. The No replies are accused of conflating understanding a proposition with believing/knowing it true.

Unresolved nuances that remain:
* The precise definition of ‘understand’ at issue: formal/parsing/compositional intelligibility vs contentful grasp/ability to evaluate the universal claim as a substantive proposition about the domain.
* Whether Evans’ requirement is generalizability of the predicate F over the domain or generalizability of the singular mode of presentation of a; the canonical formulation ∀x[x=a → Fx] is often contrasted with the unrestricted ∀x Fx.
* Whether the step from open Fx to closed ∀x Fx is a purely conceptual closure or a further substantive epistemic step.

My current take:
Consensus requires the open schematic generalizability Fx for Fa to be thinkable. With the stipulated independent grasp of ∀, that schematic competence yields at minimum formal intelligibility / parsability of ∀x Fx. The stronger claim that GC forces belief, knowledge or contentful evaluative understanding of ∀x Fx is rejected. The weaker claim that it makes ∀x Fx intelligible as the universal closure of the schema F possesses by Fa is defended by a majority, with the most aggressive Yes advocates arguing that thin intelligibility just is understanding in Evans’ sense. The substantive/doxastic commitment to the universal claim remains not required.

I think the No camp is drawing a distinction that collapses once we keep Evans’ notion of understanding strictly conceptual.

Yes, the Generality Constraint is a condition on possession of a concept, not on belief or truth-value. To think Fa in Evans’ sense is to think of a under the mode of presentation F. That mode must be genuinely general and iterable, i.e. you must possess F as the unsaturated component F that is available for systematic redeployment. Possession of F is just possession of the open schema Fx and the capacity to substitute co-referential singular terms for x without loss of content. That is the generalizability that makes Fa thinkable at all, and in Evans’ canonical statement it shows up as the ability to entertain ∀x[x = a → Fx].

Now stipulate, as we are asked to, that you understand universal quantification. Understanding ∀ is not a mysterious extra power, it is understanding the operation that takes an intelligible open schema and forms its universal closure, and knowing what would make that closure true and what would make it false.

Once you have Fx as a genuinely general mode of presentation, and you have ∀, you have the material for ∀x Fx. The singular instance is parasitic on the general concept. If Fx were intelligible to you as a general way of thinking of objects as F, and ∀ is intelligible to you as quantification, then ∀x Fx is intelligible to you in the same sense in which Fx is intelligible: you can tell what it would mean for it to be true and what would have to be the case for it to be false, even if you believe it is false.

Understanding a proposition on this account is being able to grasp what makes it true/false and to entertain it as a proposition, not endorsing it or being warranted to assert it. The No side is right that GC does not require you to believe ∀x Fx, nor does Fa entail ∀x Fx materially, and you can perfectly well understand Fa, understand Fx, understand ∀, and believe ¬∀x Fx, e.g. Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx. That is exactly the point: understanding is not belief.

What would it be for understanding Fa to be compatible with not understanding ∀x Fx? That would be a mode of presentation of F that is general enough for substitution but somehow opaque to quantificational closure. That is precisely the non-generalizable mode Evans rules out. The open/closed split is not a principled boundary once ∀ is understood; the generalizability required for Fa is generalizability under quantification. A defective grasp of F would be one where you could affirm Fa but could not even entertain the closure of the very schema you are using.

So with quantifier competence assumed, understanding Fa is understanding F as general, and understanding F as general is understanding its universal closure. GC gives you Fx and, given an understood ∀, the intelligibility of ∀x Fx as the natural closure of that schema. It is a conceptual requirement, not a doxastic one.

reflection_text.4:
The discussion has stabilised on GC as a possession / mode-of-presentation condition, not a doxastic / truth condition.

Consensus that persists across rounds 0-3:
* To understand/think Fa in Evans’ sense is to possess F as a genuinely general, unsaturated, iterable concept. Possession = possession of the open schematic form Fx with a free variable and systematic substitutability for singular terms. This is what makes the singular thought thinkable at all.
* Canonical Evans formulation is generalisability of the subject mode of presentation, e.g. ability to entertain ∀x[x=a → Fx] and to reason with Fx as an open formula, not an unrestricted claim about the extension of F.
* GC is doxastic-neutral: Fa does not entail ∀x Fx, nor is belief/warrant/truth of the universal required. Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx is compatible with understanding Fa and possessing Fx schematically. This rules out a-indexed, egocentric/demonstrative modes of F.

Divergence that is now largely terminological:
* Open schema vs closed universal with stipulated grasp of ∀.
  - Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,15,2,3,5,7,8,9 now state: GC requires Fx open; with independent grasp of ∀ you get thin formal/compositional intelligibility / parsability of ∀x Fx as the universal closure of the intelligible schema Fx. Understanding ∀ is understanding the closure operation and what would make the closure true/false. That thin intelligibility is the Evansian notion of ‘understand’ = conceptual competence to make sense of and entertain a proposition, not endorsement.
  - Colleagues 4,6,8,9 continue to stress the primary Evansian requirement is the open schema and ∀x[x=a → Fx]; the closed universal ∀x Fx is a further substantive claim about extension. They allow thin syntactic intelligibility once ∀ is mastered but emphasise GC does not require contentful/evaluative understanding, belief, knowledge or warrant for ∀x Fx.
Both sides now concede: possession of F + possession of ∀ = compositional intelligibility of ∀x Fx; no material entailment Fa ⊢ ∀x Fx and no requirement to endorse the universal.

Key nuance repeatedly flagged:
Evans’ requirement is generalisability of the mode of presentation of a, ∀x[x=a → Fx], not necessarily unrestricted ∀x Fx. Understanding is used in two senses: formal/compositional intelligibility vs contentful/evaluative understanding/warrant/belief. Most disagreement is verbal about which sense the question intends.

Current unresolved for me:
How strictly to read “understand Fx (\forall x)”. If Fx means the open schematic form, GC clearly demands it. If it means the closed proposition ∀x Fx, the debate is between thin intelligibility/parsing given quantifier competence – now widely accepted as secured by F + ∀ – vs substantive contentful/evaluative understanding of the universal claim. With stipulated grasp of ∀, the thin sense of understanding ∀x Fx is secured as the natural closure of the schema already possessed by Fa; substantive endorsement remains unrequired.

I am tracking:
1. Schematic generalisability required for Fa → yes for Fx open, and canonically ∀x[x=a → Fx].
2. Material entailment to universal belief/truth → no.
3. With stipulated grasp of ∀, formal intelligibility of ∀x Fx is available as compositional closure; whether that counts as “understanding ∀x Fx” in Evansian sense is now framed as terminological.

No new evidence has shifted the core; the split remains between thin compositional intelligibility of closure and substantive evaluative commitment.
reflection_text.9:
The Generality Constraint is stably read as a possession / mode-of-presentation condition on conceptual competence, not on belief, truth value or warrant.

Consensus across rounds 0-3:
* To think/understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to think of a under concept F.
* That requires F to be possessed as a genuinely general, unsaturated, iterable component. Possession of F = possession of the open schema Fx with a free variable and systematic substitutability for singular terms without loss of content.
* Schematic generalisability is what makes Fa thinkable and rules out a-indexed, egocentric/demonstrative modes. Canonical Evans formulation is generalisability of the subject mode of presentation, e.g. ∀x[x=a → Fx], not an unrestricted claim about the extension of F.
* Doxastic neutral: Fa does not entail ∀x Fx; Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx is compatible with understanding Fa and possessing Fx. GC gives no belief, knowledge, warrant or truth for the unrestricted universal.

Persistent disagreement is narrowed to the sense of ‘understand’ for the closed universal ∀x Fx given stipulated grasp of ∀.

Yes / thin intelligibility camp in round 3: 1,10,11,12,13,14,15,2,3,5,7,8,9. With independent grasp of ∀, possession of the intelligible open concept Fx plus grasp of ∀ gives compositional / thin intelligibility of the closure ∀x Fx: you can parse it, state its truth conditions, entertain it as a proposition. Understanding is conceptual competence / ability to make sense of, not endorsement. They argue it is odd to allow understanding of Fx and ∀ but not their composition; Evans’ canonical generalisability already puts ∀ into the possession condition and the open schema is general only in virtue of being closable under quantification.

No / schema-only / contentful camp in round 3: 4,6,8,9 with nuance. GC gives only the open schematic form Fx and generalisability of the mode of presentation of a. With understood ∀ you can parse the string ∀x Fx syntactically/semantically, but GC does not require contentful/evaluative understanding of, or epistemic warrant for, the substantive proposition that everything is F. Understanding Fa is compatible with ¬∀x Fx. The closed universal is a further substantive claim about extension, not forced by Fa.

Intermediate nuance repeatedly maintained: distinction between thin syntactic/semantic intelligibility of the form ∀x Fx once Fx and ∀ are possessed vs substantive understanding/evaluability/commitment to the closed universal proposition. Conflation of understanding the form with believing it true is flagged as error.

Round 3 convergence: 1,10,11,12,15 explicitly concede formal/compositional intelligibility of ∀x Fx from Fx+∀, while stressing it is not a doxastic/epistemic requirement. 12,13,14 argue the “No” claim that you can understand schema and quantifier but not their combination collapses on Evans’ thin competence notion. 4,6,8,9 maintain thin intelligibility ≠ contentful grasp; GC secures schematic generalisability Fx and, with quantifier competence, thin formal intelligibility of the closure, but does not require understanding, endorsement or knowledge of the substantive closed generalisation ∀x Fx as a claim about the world.

My current leaning remains: GC decisively requires the open schema Fx; with an assumed grasp of ∀ the universal closure ∀x Fx is formally intelligible/combinatorially available – you can make sense of it, parse it, know its truth conditions – but GC does not require a doxastic or epistemic commitment to, or ability to evaluate the substantive truth of, ∀x Fx. The debate therefore turns on intended sense of ‘understand’ in the prompt: schematic competence to deploy F with a variable vs contentful grasp/evaluability of the closed universal claim. Unresolved: what the question asks for under ‘understand Fx (∀x)?’

Retained earlier points: GC is neutral on truth/warrant; Fa does not entail ∀x Fx; understanding is not endorsement; Evans’ canonical generalisability is ∀x[x=a → Fx], not ∀x Fx; non-generalizable mode is ruled out.

PUBLIC RESPONSE:

GC is a possession / mode-of-presentation condition on F, not a doxastic or truth condition on the extension of F.

To understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to think of a under a genuinely general, unsaturated, iterable concept F. Possession of F is possession of the open schematic form Fx, ‘x is F’, with a free variable and systematic redeployability with co-referential singular terms. That is the generalisability Evans canonically formulates as the ability to entertain ∀x[x=a → Fx], not as a commitment to ∀x Fx. GC is therefore doxastic-neutral: Fa does not entail ∀x Fx and Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx is compatible with understanding Fa and possessing the schema Fx.

Given by hypothesis an independent grasp of ∀, possession of the general concept F together with possession of ∀ is possession of the compositional intelligibility of the closure of the very schema you already possess. Understanding ∀ on the Evansian picture is understanding the operation that takes an intelligible open schema to its closure and what would make that closure true and what would make it false.

If Fx is intelligible and ∀ is intelligible, ∀x Fx is formally / syntactically-semantically intelligible in the thin Evansian sense: you can parse it, say what would make it true and what would make it false, and entertain it as a proposition. That is the thin conceptual competence sense of ‘understand’.

It is not Fa ⊢ ∀x Fx, nor a requirement to believe, know, be warranted for, or be able to evaluate the substantive claim that everything is F. Understanding is not endorsement. GC secures the open generalisability Fx and, with quantifier competence, the thin compositional intelligibility of the universal closure ∀x Fx as the natural closure of that schema. Substantive evaluative grasp / endorsement of the universal proposition as a claim about the world is not required by GC and is not entailed by Fa.

reflection_text.15:
The Evansian core has stabilised across rounds 0-4. GC is a possession/mode-of-presentation condition, not a doxastic/truth condition. To understand/think Fa in Evans’ sense is to think of a under F, which requires F to be possessed as a genuinely general, unsaturated, iterable Fregean component. Possession of F is possession of the open schematic form Fx / ‘x is F’ with x free, systematic substitutability for co-referential singular terms, and redeployability with arbitrary argument. Evans’ canonical formulation is generalisability of the subject mode of presentation, e.g. ability to entertain ∀x[x=a → Fx], not an unrestricted material commitment to ∀x Fx. That open generalisability makes singular thought thinkable and rules out a-indexed/egocentric/demonstrative modes.

What is secured: GC licenses the open schema Fx; Fa is parasitic on possession of F as general; GC is doxastic neutral. Fa does not entail ∀x Fx; you can understand Fa, possess Fx, and believe ¬∀x Fx, e.g. Fa ∧ ∃x ¬Fx. GC gives no belief, knowledge, warrant or truth for the unrestricted universal.

Round 4 makes thin vs contentful explicit and consolidates convergence. With the stipulated independent grasp of ∀, possession of general F plus possession of ∀ gives compositional/formal intelligibility of the closed string ∀x Fx: you can parse it, state what would make it true/false, and entertain it as a proposition with determinate truth-conditions. That is thin syntactic/semantic intelligibility, not the material inference Fa ⊢ ∀x Fx, and not a requirement to believe, know, be warranted for, or evaluatively endorse the substantive claim that everything is F.

Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,15,7,2,3,5,4,6,8,9 now converge on this possession picture: understanding Fa entails understanding F as general i.e. schema Fx and canonical generalisability ∀x[x=a→Fx]; with ∀-competence that entails the thin compositional intelligibility of ∀x Fx as universal closure of that schema. Understanding is not endorsement.

The persistent tension is purely terminological about what is packed into ‘understand ∀x Fx’. The thin camp holds that syntactic combinability of an understood predicate with an understood quantifier, on Evans’ competence/ability-to-make-sense-of notion of understand, just is understanding the closure. The thick camp stresses that that is formal/parsability, not contentful/evaluative understanding of the substantive universal proposition as a claim about the world; the move from intelligible schema to substantive universal claim is a material inference about the world, not forced by GC.

I retain: GC gives Fx open schema. Given independent ∀-competence, ∀x Fx is formally/compositionally intelligible in the thin Evansian sense, but GC alone does not entail doxastic/epistemic commitment or contentful evaluative understanding/endorsement of the substantive proposition that everything is F. Consensus is that thin intelligibility is secured; disagreement is verbal whether that thin availability counts as ‘understand ∀x Fx’ in Evans’ sense, or whether Evans requires only open schema Fx and canonical generalisation ∀x[x=a→Fx]. Classic demonstration/egocentric counterexamples are blocked by lack of generalizable mode of presentation, not by inability to utter a universal.
